title: Resume Preparation
description: Building a resume, portfolio, and online presence that gets a candidate past the screen and into the interview.
blurb: Building a resume, portfolio, and online presence that gets a candidate past the screen and into the interview.
careerApplications: The resume and portfolio are the gate every application must pass before any human even considers the candidate — polish here directly determines interview volume.

beginner: ATS optimization: passing the automated screen
Portfolio creation: showing, not just telling

lessons.title: Resume fundamentals: structure & content
objectives: Structure a resume that a recruiter can scan in under 10 seconds
Explain how scannable structure changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect scannable structure with outcome-focused bullets and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A resume gets scanned, not read, in the first pass — often under 10 seconds. Structure matters as much as content: a clear header, a tight skills section, and experience/projects described with concrete outcomes ('reduced query time by 40%') rather than vague duties ('worked on backend features').
examples:
# weak: 'Worked on the backend of a web application'
# strong: 'Built a REST API serving 10k+ daily requests, reducing average response time by 35%'
commonMistakes: Listing job duties instead of outcomes — 'responsible for X' tells a recruiter what you were assigned, not what you actually accomplished or how well you did it.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the single highest-leverage document in the entire job search — every other prep track feeds into what this document claims.
lessons.explain: A resume gets scanned, not read, in the first pass — often under 10 seconds. Structure matters as much as content: a clear header, a tight skills section, and experience/projects described with concrete outcomes ('reduced query time by 40%') rather than vague duties ('worked on backend features').

# strong: 'Built a REST API serving 10k+ daily requests, reducing average response time by 35%'

lessons.title: ATS optimization: passing the automated screen
objectives: Format and word a resume to survive automated screening
Explain how ATS parsing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect ATS parsing with keyword matching and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Many companies run resumes through an ATS (Applicant Tracking System) before a human ever sees them — software that parses text and often filters by keyword match against the job description.
examples:
# job description says: 'Experience with React.js and RESTful APIs required'
# resume should include those EXACT terms if true, not just close synonyms like 'frontend frameworks' and 'web services'
commonMistakes: Using a visually elaborate template with text boxes, columns, or icons that an ATS parser mangles into unreadable, out-of-order text — simpler, more standard formatting is safer for the.
lessons.careerRelevance: A resume that never survives the ATS never reaches a human, regardless of how strong the actual candidate is.
lessons.explain: Many companies run resumes through an ATS (Applicant Tracking System) before a human ever sees them — software that parses text and often filters by keyword match against the job description.
lessons.example:
# job description says: 'Experience with React.js and RESTful APIs required'
# resume should include those EXACT terms if true, not just close synonyms like 'frontend frameworks' and 'web services'

lessons.title: Portfolio creation: showing, not just telling
objectives: Build a portfolio that lets evidence speak instead of just claims
Explain how evidence over claims changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect evidence over claims with project curation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A resume CLAIMS skill; a portfolio (a personal site, deployed projects, a curated GitHub) PROVES it with evidence a reader can actually inspect.
examples:
# a portfolio entry that actually persuades:
# project name + one-line problem statement + live demo link + README covering
# key decisions and trade-offs + a screenshot -- not just a bare repo link
commonMistakes: Listing 15 half-finished tutorial-following projects with no individual context — quantity without depth or documentation reads as unfinished, not prolific.
lessons.careerRelevance: A portfolio is frequently what actually gets discussed in an interview, far more than the resume bullet points themselves.
lessons.explain: A resume CLAIMS skill; a portfolio (a personal site, deployed projects, a curated GitHub) PROVES it with evidence a reader can actually inspect.
lessons.example:
# a portfolio entry that actually persuades:
# project name + one-line problem statement + live demo link + README covering
# key decisions and trade-offs + a screenshot -- not just a bare repo link

lessons.title: Building a strong GitHub profile
objectives: Curate a GitHub profile that reads well to a technical reviewer
Explain how pinned repositories changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pinned repositories with README quality and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A recruiter or engineer will often click through to GitHub before or during an interview loop — a profile with pinned, well-named repositories, clear READMEs, and a sensible commit history (from the Git & GitHub track) reads as someone who ships real, maintained work.
examples:
# pin your 4-6 BEST repos explicitly (GitHub lets you choose)
# make sure each pinned repo has: a real README, a working demo/screenshot if applicable,
# and reasonably recent, real commit activity -- not a single 'initial commit'
commonMistakes: Leaving GitHub's default repo ordering (most recently updated) instead of deliberately pinning your strongest work — a reviewer may see an old throwaway script before your best project.
lessons.careerRelevance: Technical interviewers frequently browse a candidate's GitHub directly, making it a real extension of the resume, not a side detail.
lessons.explain: A recruiter or engineer will often click through to GitHub before or during an interview loop — a profile with pinned, well-named repositories, clear READMEs, and a sensible commit history (from the Git & GitHub track) reads as someone who ships real, maintained work.

lessons.title: LinkedIn optimization
objectives: Optimize a LinkedIn profile for both recruiter search and human review
Explain how headline optimization changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect headline optimization with searchability vs readability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: LinkedIn serves two audiences: recruiters SEARCHING by keyword (so your headline and skills section should include the exact terms you want to be found for) and humans actually READING your profile once found (so your About section should read like a coherent narrative, not a keyword dump).
examples:
# weak headline: 'Software Engineer'
# stronger: 'Backend Software Engineer | Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL | Building scalable APIs'
# -- searchable keywords AND a clear specialization, in one line
commonMistakes: Leaving a LinkedIn profile mostly blank or unchanged since account creation — an incomplete profile is directly filtered out of many recruiter searches before a human ever considers the.
lessons.careerRelevance: A significant share of real interview opportunities, especially for internships, originate from inbound recruiter outreach on LinkedIn, not just applications.
lessons.explain: LinkedIn serves two audiences: recruiters SEARCHING by keyword (so your headline and skills section should include the exact terms you want to be found for) and humans actually READING your profile once found (so your About section should read like a coherent narrative, not a keyword dump).

# weak headline: 'Software Engineer'
# stronger: 'Backend Software Engineer | Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL | Building scalable APIs'
# -- searchable keywords AND a clear specialization, in one line

lessons.title: Tailoring a resume per application
objectives: Adjust a resume's emphasis and keywords for a specific job posting
Explain how tailored emphasis changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tailored emphasis with keyword alignment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A single generic resume sent everywhere underperforms a resume deliberately tailored per application — not rewritten from scratch each time, but with emphasis, keyword alignment, and bullet ordering adjusted to mirror what THIS specific job description prioritizes.
examples:
# job description emphasizes 'distributed systems' and 'API design' repeatedly
# -> reorder/reword your bullets to foreground exactly those experiences first,
# even if your resume also has other, less-relevant experience further down
commonMistakes: Sending the identical resume to every application regardless of role focus — small, targeted adjustments measurably improve response rates for a modest time cost per application.
lessons.careerRelevance: Tailoring is a repeatable, high-ROI habit that compounds across every application in a real job search.
lessons.explain: A single generic resume sent everywhere underperforms a resume deliberately tailored per application — not rewritten from scratch each time, but with emphasis, keyword alignment, and bullet ordering adjusted to mirror what THIS specific job description prioritizes.
lessons.example:

# -> reorder/reword your bullets to foreground exactly those experiences first,
# even if your resume also has other, less-relevant experience further down

lessons.title: Common resume mistakes
objectives: Identify and fix the most frequent resume mistakes
Explain how typos/inconsistency changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect typos/inconsistency with length discipline and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The most common, avoidable mistakes: typos and inconsistent formatting (a strong signal of carelessness to a reviewer), burying the most relevant experience below less relevant older material, resumes over 1-2 pages for early-career candidates, and vague buzzwords ('hardworking team player') with no concrete evidence behind them.
examples:
# vague, unsupported claim: 'Excellent problem solver and team player'
# fix: replace with a specific, evidenced example --
# 'Diagnosed and fixed a production memory leak, reducing server restarts by 90%'
commonMistakes: Treating buzzword-heavy language as a substitute for specific, evidenced accomplishments — reviewers routinely discount unsupported adjectives.
lessons.careerRelevance: Catching these mistakes before submission is entirely free — this lesson's checklist directly prevents avoidable rejections.
lessons.explain: The most common, avoidable mistakes: typos and inconsistent formatting (a strong signal of carelessness to a reviewer), burying the most relevant experience below less relevant older material, resumes over 1-2 pages for early-career candidates, and vague buzzwords ('hardworking team player') with no concrete evidence behind them.
lessons.example:
# vague, unsupported claim: 'Excellent problem solver and team player'
# fix: replace with a specific, evidenced example --

lessons.title: The resume review checklist
objectives: Apply a systematic final checklist before submitting a resume
Explain how pre-submission checklist changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pre-submission checklist with external review and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before submitting: does every bullet show an outcome, not just a duty? Does it mirror the target job description's key terms?
examples:
# a genuinely useful pre-submit checklist:
# [ ] every bullet has a measurable/concrete outcome
# [ ] key terms from the job description appear naturally
# [ ] simple, ATS-safe formatting
# [ ] zero typos (read aloud + a second reviewer)
# [ ] most relevant experience appears first
commonMistakes: Submitting a resume immediately after writing it with no second pass or outside reviewer — a fresh set of eyes catches errors and unclear phrasing the writer has become blind to.
lessons.careerRelevance: A consistent final-check habit is a small, repeatable discipline with an outsized effect on interview conversion rate.
lessons.explain: Before submitting: does every bullet show an outcome, not just a duty? Does it mirror the target job description's key terms?
lessons.example:
# a genuinely useful pre-submit checklist:
# [ ] every bullet has a measurable/concrete outcome
# [ ] key terms from the job description appear naturally
# [ ] simple, ATS-safe formatting
# [ ] zero typos (read aloud + a second reviewer)
# [ ] most relevant experience appears first

lessons.title: Quantifying your achievements with real numbers
objectives: Turn vague resume claims into specific, quantified evidence
Explain how quantifying achievements changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect quantifying achievements with specific numbers and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: "Improved performance" is vague and unconvincing. "Reduced page load time by 40%, cutting bounce rate by 15%" is specific, verifiable-sounding, and memorable.
examples:
# vague: 'Improved the checkout process'
# quantified: 'Redesigned checkout flow, reducing cart abandonment from 68% to 51%'
commonMistakes: Writing achievements as vague responsibilities ('worked on X') instead of quantified outcomes ('achieved Y, measured by Z').
lessons.careerRelevance: Quantified achievements are consistently what recruiters and hiring managers say they scan for first.
lessons.explain: "Improved performance" is vague and unconvincing. "Reduced page load time by 40%, cutting bounce rate by 15%" is specific, verifiable-sounding, and memorable.

quiz.q: A resume bullet is strongest when it shows:
options: a list of duties
a concrete, measurable outcome
as many buzzwords as possible
the exact hours worked

quiz.q: ATS optimization mainly means:
options: adding more graphics
using simple, parseable formatting and matching job-description keywords
writing a longer resume
using a colorful template

quiz.q: A strong portfolio generally favors:
options: as many projects as possible, regardless of completion
2-3 polished, well-documented projects over many unfinished ones
projects with no README
private repositories only

quiz.q: Tailoring a resume per application primarily means:
options: rewriting it completely from scratch every time
adjusting emphasis and keywords to match the specific job description
making it longer
removing all prior experience

quiz.q: The resume review checklist is best used:
options: only once, when first written
as a final, repeatable gate before every submission
only for the first application
after the interview is over

quiz.q: What does 'the 10-second test' for a resume mean?
options: how long it takes to print
whether a reader can grasp your key qualifications in a very quick skim
the required font size
how long the interview should last

quiz.q: Why prefer outcome-focused bullets over responsibility-focused ones?
options: outcomes are less important than responsibilities
outcomes demonstrate impact and results, which is more compelling than just listing duties performed
responsibility-focused bullets are always better
this distinction doesn't matter to recruiters

quiz.q: What does ATS stand for?
options: Automated Talent Screening
Applicant Tracking System
Advanced Text Scanner
Assessment Tracking Software

quiz.q: Why does simple, parseable formatting matter for ATS?
options: formatting has no effect on ATS
complex formatting (tables, images, unusual fonts) can prevent an ATS from correctly extracting your information
ATS systems only reject resumes with too much formatting
ATS systems always parse every format identically

quiz.q: What does keyword matching in ATS systems look for?
options: only the applicant's name
terms from the job description appearing in your resume, since many ATS systems rank or filter based on this
a synonym for font matching
only years of experience

quiz.q: Why prioritize evidence over claims in a portfolio?
options: claims are always more persuasive
concrete evidence (real projects, code, outcomes) is more convincing than unsupported self-description
evidence and claims are equally weighted always
portfolios shouldn't include evidence

quiz.q: What does project curation for a portfolio mean?
options: including every project you've ever done
selecting and presenting your strongest, most relevant projects rather than everything indiscriminately
curation only matters for design portfolios
avoiding any project selection at all

quiz.q: Why does README quality matter for a GitHub portfolio?
options: READMEs are rarely read
a clear README helps a reviewer quickly understand what a project does and why it matters, without reading all the code
READMEs only matter for very large projects
README quality has no bearing on how a project is perceived

quiz.q: What does commit history 'as evidence' mean?
options: commit history is irrelevant to evaluators
a consistent, meaningful commit history can demonstrate real, sustained work and good practices, not just a final code dump
commit messages are never checked by anyone
only the number of commits matters, not their content

quiz.q: Why optimize a LinkedIn headline?
options: headlines have no effect on visibility
a clear, keyword-relevant headline improves how easily recruiters find and understand your profile in search
LinkedIn headlines are purely decorative
only your most recent job title should ever appear there

quiz.q: What tension exists between searchability and readability on LinkedIn?
options: there's no real tension
packing in keywords for search can make a profile awkward to read for actual humans, requiring a balance
searchability and readability are the same thing
only readability matters, search behavior is irrelevant

quiz.q: Why tailor a resume per application rather than sending one generic version?
options: tailoring wastes time with no real benefit
different roles emphasize different skills, and reflecting the specific job's priorities improves relevance and ATS matching
recruiters never notice tailored vs generic resumes
one generic resume is always equally effective everywhere

quiz.q: What does bullet reordering across applications accomplish?
options: nothing meaningful
surfacing your most relevant experience for THIS specific role near the top, rather than a fixed generic order
reordering has no effect on how resumes are read
bullets should never be reordered

quiz.q: Why are typos and inconsistencies particularly damaging on a resume?
options: they have minimal real impact
they can signal carelessness to a reviewer, even if unrelated to your actual skills, in a document meant to represent your best work
typos are expected and ignored by recruiters
consistency doesn't matter as long as content is accurate

quiz.q: Why avoid buzzwords without supporting evidence?
options: buzzwords always strengthen a resume
unsupported buzzwords ('detail-oriented', 'hard worker') are vague and unconvincing without concrete evidence backing them up
evidence is unnecessary if the buzzword sounds impressive
buzzwords are required by ATS systems

quiz.q: Why maintain length discipline on a resume?
options: longer resumes are always better
excessive length can bury your strongest points and signal poor prioritization, especially early in a career
length has no effect on how a resume is received
resumes should always be exactly one specific length regardless of experience

quiz.q: Why get external review of your resume before submitting it?
options: external review is unnecessary if you're confident
a fresh perspective often catches unclear phrasing, typos, or missing context you're too close to notice yourself
external reviewers are never more effective than self-review
external review can only be done by professional resume writers

quiz.q: Why use a systematic final-pass checklist before submitting a resume?
options: checklists are unnecessary busywork
having a systematic pass reduces the chance of missing an obvious formatting, spelling, or content issue right before it matters most
checklists guarantee a resume gets an interview
final review has no measurable benefit

quiz.q: Why include specific, quantified numbers in resume achievements?
options: numbers are decorative and don't add real value
specific numbers make claims verifiable-seeming and memorable, distinguishing them from vague, unsupported claims
numbers are only relevant for finance roles
vague claims are always equally persuasive

quiz.q: What is a strong example of quantifying an achievement?
options: 'Worked on the checkout process'
'Reduced cart abandonment from 68% to 51% by redesigning the checkout flow'
'Responsible for checkout'
'Helped with checkout improvements'

quiz.q: Why does 'showing, not just telling' matter in a portfolio?
options: telling is always more effective than showing
concrete demonstrations (real code, live projects, documented outcomes) are more convincing than simply asserting your skills
showing and telling are equally weak approaches
portfolios should rely entirely on self-description

quiz.q: Why pin specific repositories on a GitHub profile?
options: pinning has no effect on how a profile is viewed
pinned repos are the first things a visitor sees, so they should showcase your strongest, most representative work
GitHub automatically selects the best repos to feature
pinning is only relevant for large open-source projects

quiz.q: What is a risk of over-relying on ATS keyword stuffing?
options: there's no risk, more keywords are always better
excessive, unnatural keyword stuffing can make a resume read poorly for the human reviewer who eventually sees it, even if it passes ATS
ATS systems always penalize keyword usage entirely
keyword stuffing improves readability

quiz.q: Why might recruiter search behavior matter when optimizing a LinkedIn profile?
options: recruiters never search LinkedIn directly
understanding what terms recruiters actually search for helps you include those terms naturally where they'll be found
search behavior is completely unpredictable and not worth considering
recruiter search only matters for entry-level roles

quiz.q: Why is a resume's structure (clear sections, scannable layout) important?
options: structure has no real effect on how a resume is received
a scannable structure helps a time-pressed reviewer quickly find the information most relevant to their decision
structure only matters for creative-industry resumes
unstructured resumes are equally effective
